protections: P1 authorization: a URL-driven cover download is only attempted for callers holding the upload role; the form field is also hidden unless role_upload and config_uploading are set (cps/editbooks.py:795-796, cps/templates/book_edit.html:101, cps/admin.py:110).

P2 response validation: the downloaded body must present an image content-type before it is stored; with ImageMagick the allowlist is exact-match, without it the test is a substring test on the string 'image/jpeg' (cps/helper.py:629-634, cps/helper.py:648-651).
P3 destination validation (absent): the outbound request is made to whatever URL the caller supplies, with no scheme, host, private-address or redirect-target check (cps/helper.py:585-588).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The field already has a permission gate (cps/editbooks.py:795-796) and is only rendered to uploaders (cps/templates/book_edit.html:101), so the route looks hardened; the fetcher itself never looks at the destination.

requests follows 3xx by default and this call passes no allow_redirects=False (cps/helper.py:587), so a check of the submitted string alone is bypassed by a public URL that redirects to an internal one; redirects are normal for image/CDN sources, so the gap reads as a non-issue.

The hostname is resolved by the socket layer when the request is made, i.e. after any lexical test, so a name that resolves (or re-resolves) to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 passes a host-string check; a hostname comparison looks like a complete fix, which makes the resolved-vs-lexical gap easy to overlook.

A server-side role test already exists on this exact field and the UI only offers it when uploads are enabled, so the entry point looks guarded; but the stored config value config_uploading/g.allow_upload is never re-checked here, while the sibling /upload route does check it (cps/editbooks.py:1026), so a direct POST still reaches the fetch while uploads are globally disabled.

The value in the cover_url field can be written by a metadata-provider response rather than typed by the user (get_meta.js copies the provider's cover link into the field), and providers are treated as trusted, so a fix that only sanitises hand-typed input or only touches the template misses provider-supplied destinations.

The same branch uses the relative sentinel '/static/generic_cover.jpg' to remove a cover without any request; a strict rule that only accepts absolute http(s) URLs would break cover removal, so a fixer may either exempt the sentinel (correct) or weaken/skip the URL rule to keep it (wrong). This is a coupled must-keep-working value, not a missing guard.

conflicts.what: The natural destination allowlist (absolute http/https, public address) rejects the relative sentinel '/static/generic_cover.jpg' that must keep clearing book.has_cover without fetching (cps/editbooks.py:797-798); the sentinel test has to run before any new URL rule.

Refusing redirects outright (the easy redirect fix) breaks legitimate cover URLs that are served through a redirecting CDN, which is the common case for the providers in T5 (cps/metadata_provider/google.py:44 rewrites http to https); the fix should re-validate the location instead of refusing redirects.

fairness_risks: A blanket private/link-local block breaks the legitimate case of fetching covers from a LAN host (another machine on the same network); the rule has to distinguish loopback/link-local from ordinary RFC1918 hosts, or be configurable.
Blocking localhost outright breaks self-hosted deployments where covers are served by a local content server on the same machine.
Cover removal via the relative sentinel '/static/generic_cover.jpg' (cps/editbooks.py:797) is a legitimate non-URL value in the same field and must not require a fetch or an absolute URL.

Covers are frequently served as application/octet-stream or with parameters; the existing allowlist already rejects those (cps/helper.py:632, cps/helper.py:649), so tightening content-type further would refuse legitimate images.

The upload role is a legitimate permission for normal users; requiring admin/edit rights in addition would break the intended editor-with-upload workflow (cps/editbooks.py:795, cps/editbooks.py:64-75).

design.why: The best available design would pair the reported sink (T1) with the two bypass shapes a literal-URL check leaves open (T2 redirect, T3 resolved-vs-lexical) and with the under-checked entry gate (T4) and the coupled sentinel (T6). But T1, T2, T3, T4 and T5 are all closed by a fix at a single site: one safe-fetch wrapper in cps/helper.py:585-590 (validate scheme/destination, disable or re-validate redirects, pin the resolved address) also moots T4 and T5, because the fetch is only reachable through cps/editbooks.py:800. Grouping therefore yields two entries, of which only one ([T1,T2,T3,T4,T5]) is a missing-protection group; [T6] is a coupled must-keep-working constraint, not a guard. So the checkout offers one independent missing-protection group, not the 3-5 independent places a stacked task needs; the only other outbound-request sites are admin-configured or fed by trusted APIs (updater, LDAP, SMTP, Gmail token_uri), so they cannot be used fairly. This candidate is a workable single-trap SSRF task but not a stack.
